cls: Osmotic laxative liquid preparation (70% sugar-alcohol solution); oral/rectal vehicle
pharm: A 70% aqueous solution of sorbitol that acts as a hyperosmotic laxative when given orally or rectally, drawing water into the bowel; also used diluted as a pharmaceutical vehicle and sweetened liquid base.
quick: Oral: 30-150 mL of the 70% solution (commonly 30 mL); rectal: 120 mL of a 25-30% solution
Not meal-dependent; may be taken on an empty stomach
Poorly absorbed, locally acting; acceptable for occasional laxative use when needed
No adjustment; avoid in hereditary fructose intolerance
Bowel response; hydration/electrolytes with heavy or repeated use
summary: Sorbitol Solution is the liquid preparation of sorbitol, typically supplied as a 70% aqueous solution and diluted to 25-30% for rectal use. Given orally it is an osmotic (hyperosmotic) laxative for occasional constipation - usually 30 mL, up to 30-150 mL, of the 70% solution; rectally it is given as a 120 mL enema of 25-30% solution. The same solution serves as a sweetened liquid vehicle and excipient in pharmaceutical preparations. It is poorly absorbed and works locally in the gut, so precise systemic pharmacokinetics are not meaningful. It is not an FDA new-drug-approval product; dosing follows BNF/EMA/pharmacopoeial monographs. Historically used as the vehicle for sodium polystyrene sulfonate, but the FDA warns this combination has caused colonic necrosis. Avoid in hereditary fructose intolerance.
indications: Occasional constipation - oral osmotic laxative (70% solution)
Occasional constipation - rectal osmotic laxative (25-30% solution enema)
Pharmaceutical liquid vehicle, sweetener, and humectant in oral preparations
Vehicle to facilitate oral administration/passage of certain agents
Historically, liquid vehicle for sodium polystyrene sulfonate suspension (now discouraged - see pearls)

dosage.d: 30-150 mL of 70% solution as a single dose (commonly 30 mL of 70% solution)
120 mL of 25-30% solution as a single retention enema
dosage.n: Dilute the 70% solution to 25-30% for rectal use

dosage.d: Approximately 2 mL/kg of 70% solution as a single dose
Quantity sufficient as a liquid base/sweetening vehicle in compounded or manufactured preparations

admin: Oral laxative: administer the 70% solution and follow with adequate water
Rectal use: dilute to 25-30% and give as a 120 mL retention enema
Allow time for the osmotic effect (oral relief in hours; rectal faster)
As a vehicle, dilute appropriately - do NOT combine with sodium polystyrene sulfonate (colonic necrosis risk)
Do not use in patients with hereditary fructose intolerance
moa: Sorbitol Solution delivers sorbitol, a slowly and incompletely absorbed sugar alcohol, to the intestinal lumen. The unabsorbed sorbitol is osmotically active and draws water into the bowel, increasing intraluminal fluid and stool water content; this softens stool, increases luminal volume, and stimulates peristalsis to produce a laxative effect. Given rectally as a dilute solution, the same hyperosmotic mechanism acts locally in the rectum and distal colon. When used as a vehicle or sweetener, the solution functions as an osmotically active, sweet liquid base rather than through any pharmacologic receptor action. Absorbed sorbitol is metabolized hepatically to fructose and then glucose.

absolute: Intestinal obstruction, ileus, or fecal impaction with obstruction
Undiagnosed acute abdominal pain or suspected perforation
relative: Concomitant sodium polystyrene sulfonate (colonic necrosis risk - avoid combination)
Active inflammatory bowel disease or fragile gut mucosa
Rectal use with rectal bleeding or recent rectal/colonic surgery
monitor: Time to bowel response and adequacy of evacuation
Hydration and electrolytes with repeated or large-volume use
Local rectal irritation with enema use

preg: The solution is locally acting and poorly absorbed, so systemic exposure is minimal. It is generally regarded as acceptable for occasional laxative use during pregnancy when a laxative is required. Evidence is from pharmacopoeial/formulary monographs rather than dedicated pregnancy studies.
lact: Because sorbitol is poorly absorbed and stays largely within the gut, meaningful passage into breast milk is not expected; the solution is considered compatible with breastfeeding for occasional laxative use.
renal: No dosage adjustment is required for laxative use. If a sorbitol-containing solution is used in large irrigation volumes, monitor fluid and electrolyte status in patients with renal impairment.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment for laxative use. Any absorbed sorbitol is metabolized hepatically (to fructose then glucose); the solution must be avoided in hereditary fructose intolerance, where it can cause hypoglycemia and hepatic injury.

major: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate) - using sorbitol solution as the suspension vehicle has caused colonic/intestinal necrosis; FDA warns against co-administration
moderate: Other laxatives - additive osmotic/cathartic effect; risk of dehydration and electrolyte loss
Concurrently swallowed oral drugs - osmotic diarrhea may reduce their absorption
minor: Other dietary polyols (mannitol, xylitol) - additive gastrointestinal osmotic load
interactions.food: Not meal-dependent; high dietary polyol intake adds to osmotic gastrointestinal effect.
interactions.diagnostics: Excessive or prolonged use may produce fluid/electrolyte changes on serum chemistry.

serious: Dehydration and electrolyte imbalance from excessive use
Colonic/intestinal necrosis when used as a vehicle with sodium polystyrene sulfonate
rare: Hypoglycemia and hepatic injury in hereditary fructose intolerance
Local rectal irritation with enema use
emergency: Bowel necrosis or perforation (especially with sodium polystyrene sulfonate)
Acute metabolic decompensation in fructose intolerance

monitoring: Bowel response and resolution of constipation
Hydration and electrolytes with frequent or large-volume use
Severe abdominal pain, distension, or rectal bleeding
Local tolerance of the rectal preparation
counsel: This is a liquid laxative that softens stool by drawing water into the bowel - drink plenty of fluids
Measure the 70% solution carefully; for enema use it is diluted to a weaker (25-30%) solution
Gas, bloating, and loose stools are common and usually mild
Do not use for more than a few days for constipation without medical advice
Avoid if you have hereditary fructose intolerance; seek care for severe pain or rectal bleeding
pk: Oral effect generally within several hours; rectal enema effect more rapid
Acts locally in the gut; poorly and slowly absorbed (no clinically meaningful systemic peak)
Not well characterized as a systemic drug; absorbed fraction is rapidly metabolized in the liver
Effect persists until bowel evacuation is complete
Store at room temperature; keep tightly closed and protect from freezing per product labeling
pearls: Supplied as a 70% solution for oral use and diluted to 25-30% for rectal enema use
Sorbitol is not a standard FDA new-drug-approval product; dosing and uses here follow BNF / EMA / pharmacopoeial monographs (Martindale, MedlinePlus, DailyMed enema products)
FDA WARNING: do NOT use sorbitol solution as the vehicle for sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate) - associated with colonic necrosis
Poorly absorbed osmotic agent acting locally; precise systemic pharmacokinetic values are not meaningful and should not be assumed
Contraindicated in hereditary fructose intolerance; also widely used as a sweetened liquid vehicle/excipient
missed: Sorbitol Solution is taken as needed for constipation rather than on a fixed schedule, so there is no missed-dose concern. If a dose does not produce a bowel movement, avoid immediately repeating large doses and seek advice if constipation persists.
overdose: Taking too much of the solution causes profuse osmotic diarrhea with cramping, which can lead to dehydration and electrolyte disturbances (e.g., hypernatremia, hypokalemia). Management is supportive: discontinue, rehydrate, and correct electrolytes. In hereditary fructose intolerance, even modest amounts can cause hypoglycemia and hepatic injury requiring urgent treatment.
